relevant_findings.topic: Four distinct metal substrate types with different chemistry
relevant_findings.finding: Exterior metal painting covers four substrate types with fundamentally different coating chemistry requirements: (1) Carbon steel/wrought iron — highly susceptible to rust, requires corrosion-inhibitive primers (DTM acrylic, DTM alkyd, zinc-rich, or epoxy). (2) Aluminum — forms Al2O3 oxide in 15 minutes after cleaning that resists adhesion; requires immediate priming after surface prep and flexible coatings for thermal expansion. (3) Galvanized steel — sacrificial zinc layer ages through three states (newly galvanized with passivation oils, partially weathered with white rust, fully weathered with stable patina); oil/alkyd coatings are PROHIBITED due to saponification. (4) Stainless steel — rarely painted, slick surface requiring etch primer if coated.

relevant_findings.topic: SSPC-SP 1 solvent clean is MANDATORY first step for ALL metal
relevant_findings.finding: Surface preparation accounts for 60-80% of a metal coating's longevity. SSPC-SP 1 (solvent cleaning — removes oil, grease, dirt) is the mandatory first step for ALL metal substrates regardless of subsequent prep. If SP 1 is skipped, mechanical prep (sanding, grinding) smears oils deeper into the surface, causing adhesion failure under the new coating. This is the single most critical process step in metal painting.

relevant_findings.topic: Structural rust is a HARD STOP — outside painting scope
relevant_findings.finding: Surface rust (thin, flaky oxide layer on carbon steel/wrought iron) is treatable through mechanical or chemical removal. Structural rot (deep pitting, crumbling metal, loss of cross-section) is NOT treatable by painting. Structural rot requires welding, reinforcement, or replacement — it is outside the scope of painting and must be flagged for the client as a prerequisite repair. Painting over structural rot is guaranteed premature failure.

Alkyd/oil-based primers and coatings react chemically with the zinc layer on galvanized steel through saponification — alkaline zinc converts paint esters into soft, soap-like substance, causing coating to peel in large sheets. This is a catastrophic, irreversible failure. ONLY specialized acrylic DTM primers, etch/wash primers, or epoxy primers are acceptable on galvanized surfaces. This must be enforced as a material blocker rule.

Aluminum forms a dense, transparent Al2O3 oxide layer within 15 minutes of surface cleaning. This oxide is protective but resists paint adhesion. After cleaning/abrading aluminum, primer MUST be applied within 15 minutes before oxide reforms. This is a critical SOP sequencing constraint — clean small sections, prime immediately, then move to the next section. Do not clean the entire surface and then go back to prime.

relevant_findings.topic: Aluminum thermal expansion requires flexible coatings
relevant_findings.finding: Aluminum has high thermal expansion — a 50-foot aluminum gutter can move over 0.75 inches during a 100-degree F temperature swing. Rigid/brittle coatings (alkyd, standard epoxy) crack and separate at expansion joints, fastener points, and seams. Aluminum substrates require flexible acrylic coatings and flexible acrylic DTM primers. Light LRV (Light Reflectance Value) colors reduce thermal cycling amplitude.

relevant_findings.topic: Rust conversion vs mechanical removal — life expectancy tradeoff
relevant_findings.finding: Two approaches to surface rust on steel/iron: (1) Rust conversion — phosphoric/tannic acid transforms iron oxide into stable ferric phosphate/tannate. Efficient and ideal for intricate structures (scrollwork, balusters) where blasting is impossible. BUT only treats top layer of rust, rough finish, and has only 1-3 year coating life. (2) Mechanical removal — abrasives/grinders to bare metal. Creates smooth, stable surface with uniform coating thickness and 4-5x longer protection life than conversion. Extremely labor-intensive. Choice is driven by surface complexity and access.

relevant_findings.topic: Multi-component spec with different UOMs per item
relevant_findings.finding: Exterior metal painting is component-based, not field-area-based. Four paintable item types: (1) Metal railings (LF) — porch/stair railings, balusters, measured linearly. (2) Gutters and downspouts (LF) — measured linearly per run. (3) Ornamental iron (EA or LF) — decorative elements, measured by piece or run depending on configuration. (4) Miscellaneous discrete items (EA) — mailbox posts, light poles, utility covers, misc hardware. Each component has different production rates, complexity profiles, and access conditions.

relevant_findings.topic: Profile complexity is the primary labor multiplier
relevant_findings.finding: Metal surface complexity drives production rate multipliers: Standard (simple pickets, straight gutters) = 1.0x baseline. Moderate (multi-story, minor decorative elements, multi-plane profiles) = 1.5x. Ornate (historic ironwork, hand-forged scrollwork, intricate patterns) = 2.0-3.0x. Complexity affects both prep and coating tasks — intricate profiles require more brush detail work, more prep time per unit, and more material per unit due to surface area increase and hard-to-reach areas.

relevant_findings.topic: Primer system selection driven by substrate type
relevant_findings.finding: Metal primer selection is substrate-dependent: Carbon steel/iron — DTM acrylic (UV stable, flexible, flash-rust resistant), DTM alkyd (superior wetting, becomes brittle), zinc-rich (galvanic protection for critical steel), or epoxy (surface-tolerant, no UV resistance — must topcoat). Aluminum — etch/wash primer (phosphoric acid etches slick surface) or acrylic bonding primer. Galvanized — etch/wash primer (T-wash or phosphoric acid), acrylic bonding primer. NEVER oil/alkyd on galvanized or aluminum.

relevant_findings.topic: Galvanized steel aging states drive different prep
relevant_findings.finding: Galvanized steel has three aging states requiring different preparation: (1) Newly galvanized — passivation oils from manufacturing must be removed with solvent (SP 1), then etch primer applied for adhesion to slick zinc surface. (2) Partially weathered — loose zinc oxides ('white rust') must be removed by hand/power tool (SP 2/SP 3), then prime. (3) Fully weathered — stable zinc carbonate patina with good adhesion profile, clean and prime directly with acrylic DTM or etch primer. The aging state determines prep intensity.

relevant_findings.topic: SSPC prep level determined by substrate condition, not chosen independently
relevant_findings.finding: SSPC surface prep standards form a hierarchy of increasing aggressiveness: SP 1 (solvent clean — mandatory always) -> SP 2 (hand tool — scrapers, wire brushes) -> SP 3 (power tool — grinders, wire wheels) -> SP 7/SP 6/SP 10/SP 5 (blast — increasing thoroughness) -> SP 11 (power tool to bare metal). The appropriate level is determined by substrate condition (light surface rust = SP 2-3, heavy rust = SP 3-SP 7, critical surfaces = SP 10-11), not chosen as an independent configuration dimension.

relevant_findings.topic: This spec covers both NC and existing metal surfaces
relevant_findings.finding: Unlike masonry or siding NC specs, exterior metal painting commonly involves existing surfaces with rust, failed coatings, or aging galvanized surfaces. New construction metal (factory-primed railings, new galvanized gutters) and existing metal (rusted iron, peeling paint on railings) are both in scope. The spec name SF_METAL_EXT_v1 (no NC) reflects this dual-scope coverage. Substrate state dimension handles the branching between bare/factory-primed metal and existing metal with surface conditions.

relevant_findings.topic: Epoxy primers lack UV resistance — must be topcoated promptly
relevant_findings.finding: Epoxy primers provide excellent adhesion and surface tolerance (can adhere to marginally prepared surfaces) but have zero UV resistance. Exposed epoxy chalks and degrades within weeks of UV exposure. Epoxy primer MUST be topcoated with UV-resistant acrylic or urethane finish within the manufacturer's recoat window (typically 24-72 hours, depending on product). Exceeding the recoat window requires re-abrading the cured epoxy surface for mechanical adhesion.

condition_drivers.impact: PRIMARY CONFIGURATION DIMENSION. Drives primer selection (DTM acrylic/alkyd for steel/iron, etch primer for aluminum/galvanized, BLOCK oil/alkyd on galvanized), prep constraints (aluminum 15-min prime window, galvanized aging state), coating flexibility requirements (aluminum needs flexible acrylic), and material blocker rules.
condition_drivers.notes: This is the most critical dimension — wrong primer on wrong substrate = catastrophic failure. Stainless steel excluded from primary scope (rarely painted in residential).

condition_drivers.impact: Drives prep module and intensity. Bare metal: full prime system. Factory-primed: verify adhesion, light abrade, topcoat. Surface rust: rust removal (mechanical or conversion) + prime. Sound existing paint: clean, abrade, topcoat. Failing paint: strip to sound substrate, treat exposed metal, reprime.
condition_drivers.notes: SS_EXT_BARE_METAL and SS_EXT_PRIMED_FACTORY are NC states. SS_EXT_SURFACE_RUST, SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT_METAL, and SS_EXT_FAILING_PAINT_METAL are existing/repaint states. Structural rust is a HARD STOP, not a substrate state.

condition_drivers.impact: QT3: standard — SP 1 + SP 2/3 prep, DTM acrylic primer, two finish coats with mid-grade DTM acrylic. QT4: premium — thorough prep (SP 3 minimum), premium primer, two finish coats with premium DTM acrylic, raking light inspection between coats. QT5: superior — maximum prep (SP 3-SP 11), zinc-rich or epoxy primer on steel, premium topcoat, near-zero defect tolerance, ornamental detail work.
condition_drivers.notes: QT2 is NOT appropriate for metal work — metal prep shortcuts lead to rapid failure. QT3 is the minimum acceptable tier. QT5 applies to ornamental/architectural ironwork and high-visibility railings.

condition_drivers.impact: Labor multiplier on all tasks. Standard (1.0x): simple pickets, straight gutters, plain downspouts. Moderate (1.5x): multi-plane profiles, minor decorative elements, grouped balusters. Ornate (2.0-3.0x): historic scrollwork, hand-forged ironwork, intricate patterns with crevices and recesses. Affects both prep and application rates.
condition_drivers.notes: This is a MODIFIER, not a configuration dimension. Applied per component — a project may have standard railings and ornate gate.

condition_drivers.impact: Brush: primary method for most metal components (railings, ornamental, detail). Provides best crevice coverage and film build. Spray: for large flat areas (gutters, large flat panels). Spray_backbrush: spray + immediate back-brushing for railings/balusters to ensure crevice coverage. No roll option — rollers are ineffective on cylindrical and complex metal profiles.
condition_drivers.notes: Brush is the dominant application method for metal. Unlike wall/siding specs where spray is primary, metal's complex profiles demand brush detail work. Spray is supplemental for flat runs.

condition_drivers.impact: Height modifier on all tasks at elevation. ground=1.00, ladder=1.35, scaffold=1.60, lift=1.50. Railings at second story or higher require ladder/scaffold. Gutter work at eave height typically requires ladder. Ornamental iron on balconies may require scaffold.
condition_drivers.notes: Height modifier APPLIES to metal work — unlike deck spec where crew stands on the surface. Metal components are mounted on building structure at various elevations.

condition_drivers.impact: Mechanical removal (SP 2/3/7-11): 4-5x longer coating life, creates smooth surface for uniform film build. Higher labor cost. Rust conversion (phosphoric/tannic acid): 1-3 year coating life, efficient for intricate surfaces where mechanical prep is impractical. Lower labor cost but shorter protection. Choice driven by surface complexity and project requirements.
condition_drivers.notes: Not an independent dimension — driven by surface complexity, access, and quality tier. Ornate scrollwork may REQUIRE conversion (mechanical prep impossible in crevices). Flat rails should use mechanical removal.

quality_differences.description: Standard exterior metal. SSPC-SP 1 solvent clean + SP 2 hand tool prep (wire brush loose rust and peeling paint). DTM acrylic primer. Two finish coats with mid-grade exterior DTM acrylic. Clean lines at metal-to-substrate junctions. Standard crevice coverage — no holidays in accessible areas.
quality_differences.typical_use: Standard residential railings, gutters, downspouts. Budget-conscious metal maintenance. Factory-primed NC metal requiring topcoat only.

quality_differences.description: Premium exterior metal. SSPC-SP 1 + SP 3 power tool prep (grinders, wire wheels). Premium DTM acrylic or epoxy primer (with timely topcoat). Two finish coats with premium exterior DTM acrylic. Raking light inspection between coats. Detail brush at all crevices, fasteners, and rivets. Crisp termination lines.
quality_differences.typical_use: High-visibility railings, front entry metalwork, premium homes. Existing metal with moderate rust requiring thorough prep.

quality_differences.description: Superior exterior metal. Maximum prep — SP 3 minimum, SP 7-11 for critical steel. Zinc-rich or epoxy primer on steel for maximum corrosion protection. Premium topcoat system. Near-zero defect tolerance. Every crevice, rivet, and fastener fully coated. Multiple inspection passes. Ornamental detail perfection.
quality_differences.typical_use: Ornamental/architectural ironwork. Historic restoration. High-end estate railings. Decorative balcony ironwork. Custom metalwork where coating failure has high replacement cost.

failure_modes.name: Adhesion loss from contamination (skipped SP 1)
failure_modes.description: Oil, grease, and dirt contamination remain on the metal surface when SSPC-SP 1 solvent cleaning is skipped. Subsequent mechanical prep (sanding, grinding) smears oils deeper into the surface profile. Primer and topcoat bond to contamination layer rather than metal substrate. Coating peels in sheets within weeks to months.
failure_modes.prevention: SSPC-SP 1 solvent clean is MANDATORY first step for ALL metal — no exceptions. Solvent wipe (mineral spirits, denatured alcohol, or proprietary degreaser) before any mechanical prep. Verify clean by running white cloth across surface.
failure_modes.detection: Coating lifts easily when scraped. Peeling in large sheets rather than small chips. Greasy feel under lifted coating. Typically uniform failure across entire surface (not localized).

failure_modes.name: Saponification on galvanized steel
failure_modes.description: Oil-based or alkyd coatings react chemically with the zinc layer on galvanized steel. Alkaline zinc converts paint esters into soft, soap-like substance (saponification). Coating becomes soft, sticky, and peels in large rubbery sheets. Complete coating system failure — no repair possible without full strip and recoat with compatible system.
failure_modes.prevention: NEVER use oil/alkyd products on galvanized steel. Material blocker rule in spec. Only acrylic DTM primers, etch/wash primers, or epoxy primers on galvanized. Verify substrate identification before primer selection.
failure_modes.detection: Soft, sticky coating that strings when touched. Rubbery feel. Peeling in large sheets with soapy residue. Discoloration of coating. Typically appears within weeks of application.

failure_modes.name: Thermal cracking on aluminum
failure_modes.description: Rigid/brittle coatings (alkyd, standard epoxy, budget latex) cannot accommodate aluminum's high thermal expansion. A 50-ft gutter moves 0.75+ inches over a 100-degree F swing. Coating cracks at expansion joints, seams, and fastener points. Cracking exposes bare aluminum to moisture, and while aluminum does not rust, the aesthetic failure and coating delamination propagate from crack points.
failure_modes.prevention: Use flexible acrylic coatings on aluminum. Avoid alkyd or rigid coatings. Specify light LRV colors to reduce thermal cycling amplitude. Ensure coating system accommodates thermal movement at joints.
failure_modes.detection: Hairline cracks at seams, joints, and fastener locations. Cracks propagate during temperature extremes. Paint flaking along expansion joint lines.

failure_modes.name: Encapsulated rust from inadequate conversion
failure_modes.description: Rust converter applied over deep pitting or heavy rust only treats the top layer of oxide. Active rust beneath the converted surface layer continues to expand, eventually lifting the converted layer and coating above it. Most common when rust converter is used as a shortcut on surfaces that require mechanical removal.
failure_modes.prevention: Mechanical removal (SP 3 or higher) for deep pitting and heavy rust. Reserve rust conversion for light surface rust or intricate areas where mechanical prep is physically impossible. Never use conversion on structurally compromised metal.
failure_modes.detection: Blistering or bubbling over previously rusted areas within 1-3 years. Rust-colored staining bleeding through coating. Coating lifting at rust pocket locations.

failure_modes.name: Application defects — holidays and poor crevice coverage
failure_modes.description: Metal surfaces have complex profiles (rivets, crevices, back sides of flanges, corner joints) that are difficult to coat uniformly. 'Holidays' (missed spots) and thin spots at crevices and back-of-flange areas leave bare metal exposed to corrosion. Single missed rivet or corner becomes a failure initiation point that propagates outward.
failure_modes.prevention: Brush application primary for complex profiles. Inspect all crevices, fasteners, and back-of-flange areas. Back-brush after spray to force coating into crevices. Multiple thin coats preferred over single heavy coat for complex profiles. QT4/QT5 require detail inspection pass.
failure_modes.detection: Localized rust spots appearing at rivets, seams, and crevice locations within months. Thin film visible at corners and recesses. Rust bleeding from behind flanges.

failure_modes.name: Oxide reformation on aluminum (missed prime window)
failure_modes.description: Aluminum cleaned and abraded but not primed within 15 minutes. Dense Al2O3 oxide layer reforms, creating a slick barrier that resists primer adhesion. Coating appears initially sound but develops progressive adhesion failure under thermal cycling and moisture exposure.
failure_modes.prevention: Work in small sections — clean and prime each section within 15 minutes. Do NOT clean entire surface then return to prime. SOP must enforce sequential clean-prime workflow. Two-person crew helpful (one preps, one primes immediately behind).
failure_modes.detection: Gradual adhesion loss starting at edges and high-thermal-cycling areas. Coating can be peeled with fingernail in thin strips. Onset typically 6-12 months after application.

notes_for_materials_manager: Primer selection is SUBSTRATE-DEPENDENT — there is no single primer for all metal. Carbon steel/iron: DTM acrylic (preferred for exterior — UV stable, flexible) or DTM alkyd (superior wetting but becomes brittle). Aluminum: etch/wash primer or acrylic bonding primer. Galvanized: etch/wash primer or acrylic bonding primer. BLOCK oil/alkyd on galvanized and aluminum.
Zinc-rich primer for critical steel at QT5 — provides galvanic (sacrificial) protection. High zinc dust content. Specialty product, not standard stock.

Epoxy primer is surface-tolerant and excellent for marginal prep situations, but LACKS UV resistance. Must be topcoated within manufacturer recoat window (24-72 hours). Include recoat window flag in material notes.

DTM acrylic finish is the standard topcoat for all metal substrates. Must be exterior-grade with UV resistance. Semi-gloss or gloss sheen standard for metal (moisture shedding, durability). Satin acceptable at QT3.

Rust converter product (phosphoric acid or tannic acid based) for treating surface rust on intricate ironwork. Not a primer — must be primed after conversion. 1-3 year life expectancy vs 4-5x for mechanical removal.

Etch/wash primers contain phosphoric acid that microscopically etches slick metal surfaces (galvanized zinc, aluminum oxide). Two-component or single-component products available. T-wash (copper salt solution) for galvanized — turns zinc black to indicate proper etching.
Flexible acrylic coatings MANDATORY for aluminum. Standard rigid latex or alkyd will crack at expansion joints. Light LRV colors recommended to reduce thermal cycling.

Brush is the primary applicator for most metal work. 2-3 inch angular sash brush for railings and detail. 1-2 inch artist brush for ornamental detail at QT5. Spray tips for flat metal runs: 411-515 (small fan for controlled application on narrow surfaces).
Wire brushes (hand and power), grinding discs, and sandpaper (80-120 grit) for mechanical prep. Solvent (mineral spirits or denatured alcohol) for SP 1 cleaning. Clean rags for solvent wipe.
notes_for_sop_librarian: Module structure: setup -> protect -> SP_1_solvent_clean (MANDATORY first step, ALL metal) -> assess_condition (surface rust vs structural — HARD STOP if structural) -> mechanical_prep_or_conversion -> prime -> apply -> interstage -> finish -> cleanup -> teardown.

SSPC-SP 1 solvent clean is the ABSOLUTE FIRST TASK after protection setup. No mechanical prep before solvent clean — sanding/grinding smears oils. Use mineral spirits, denatured alcohol, or proprietary degreaser. White cloth wipe test for cleanliness.

Structural rust assessment is a HARD STOP gate. If structural rot is found (deep pitting, crumbling metal, loss of cross-section), STOP work and flag for client. Outside painting scope — requires welding/structural repair.

Aluminum prime window: 15 minutes after cleaning. SOP must enforce work-in-sections approach — clean a 3-4 LF section, prime immediately, move to next section. Two-person crew recommended for aluminum (one cleans, one primes).

Galvanized substrate identification: verify substrate type BEFORE selecting primer. Galvanized + oil/alkyd = BLOCKED. Etch primer or acrylic bonding primer only. Newly galvanized requires solvent removal of passivation oils before etch.

Rust conversion procedure: apply converter to surface rust, wait per product instructions (typically 15-30 min), verify color change (rust converts from red-brown to black). Do NOT over-apply. Prime over converted surface after full cure (24 hours typical).

Mechanical prep procedure: SP 2 (hand tool) for light rust — wire brush, scraper. SP 3 (power tool) for moderate rust — angle grinder with wire wheel or flap disc. Work to bright metal where possible. Feather edges of sound adjacent paint. Dust/debris removal before prime.
Epoxy primer recoat window: topcoat MUST be applied within manufacturer recoat window (24-72 hours). If window is exceeded, re-abrade cured epoxy surface with 120-grit before topcoat.
Caulk metal-to-masonry and metal-to-wood junctions with polyurethane sealant (flexible, paintable). Not silicone — silicone is not paintable.

Environmental SOP note: metal surfaces in direct sun can exceed 140 degrees F — do not apply coating when surface is too hot (film defects, poor cure). Morning or shaded conditions preferred for dark metal.
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Production rates by component — Railings (simple picket): 15-25 LF/hr (brush). Railings (spray_backbrush): 25-40 LF/hr. Gutters/downspouts: 100-150 LF/hr (brush or spray on straight runs). Ornamental scrollwork: 5-10 LF/hr (brush only). Misc discrete items: 15-30 min/EA depending on size.
Profile complexity multiplier applied to ALL task rates: standard 1.0x, moderate 1.5x, ornate 2.0-3.0x. This is the dominant labor driver after access type.
Prep rates — SP 1 solvent clean: 50-100 LF/hr (wipe down). SP 2 hand tool (wire brush): 20-40 LF/hr. SP 3 power tool (grinder): 10-25 LF/hr. Rust conversion (apply + wait + verify): 30-50 LF/hr.
Access modifier (FAC_EXT_ACCESS): ground=1.00, ladder=1.35, scaffold=1.60, lift=1.50. Applies to all metal tasks at elevation. Gutter work is almost always at ladder height minimum.

Coat system: 1 primer + 2 finish coats standard at QT3/QT4. QT5 may add zinc-rich primer + epoxy intermediate + acrylic topcoat (3-coat system). Factory-primed NC metal: verify adhesion, light abrade, 2 finish coats (skip primer).

Material coverage on metal: DTM acrylic primer 400-500 SF/gal (smooth metal), 300-400 SF/gal (rough/pitted). DTM acrylic topcoat 350-450 SF/gal. Spray waste factor 25-30% on narrow profiles (overspray from small targets).
Rust treatment is a SEPARATE line item from standard prep. Mechanical removal adds significant time. Conversion is faster but has shorter life. Both are in addition to SP 1 clean time.
Environmental conditions (wind, dew point, surface temp) are EXCLUDED from estimation — per established exterior spec convention.
Scaffold setup/teardown for metal at height: 1.75-2.5 hrs setup per facade, 1.0-1.5 hrs teardown per facade (2-person crew). Separate line item from metal painting tasks.
Multi-substrate projects (e.g., steel railing + aluminum gutters on same house): each substrate type may require different primer. Track primer quantities separately.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray
zones.notes: LF-based — along base of railings/structure where landscape is adjacent. Brush: drop cloth at base. Spray: tarp over plantings within overspray zone.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray
zones.notes: Adjacent walkways below railings. Brush: drop cloth at base. Spray: full tarp coverage.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray
zones.notes: House siding behind railings, near gutters. Brush work: minimal risk. Spray: plastic sheeting on siding face.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray
zones.notes: Masonry walls behind railings or near downspout runs. Tape at metal-to-masonry junction. Spray: plastic sheeting.
Exterior light fixtures mounted on or near metal components. Bag or tape over fixture.
Roof shingles at gutter line. Drop cloth or plastic along roof edge to prevent drip staining. Gutter painting specific.

protection_zones_analysis.cross_spec_protection_note: Window and door protection during metal work is NOT this spec's responsibility. Siding protection at railing-to-siding junctions IS this spec's responsibility because brush drips and spray overspray from metal work contacts siding.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: Siding behind railings or near downspout brackets. Different product system (siding paint vs DTM metal paint). Protection only — no cut-in.
Masonry wall at railing bracket mount points, downspout brackets. Different product system. Caulk at metal-to-masonry junction.
Fascia board behind gutters. Separate trim spec. Metal-to-wood junction may require caulk.
Soffit near gutter line. Separate spec. Protection only.
Concrete porch/stoop at railing base. Railing brackets mounted to concrete. Drop cloth protection.
Wood deck surface at railing post bases. Different product system (stain vs metal paint). Protection at railing-to-deck junction.

adjacency_analysis.key_finding: Metal components are mounted ON other surfaces (siding, masonry, fascia, concrete, wood). All adjacencies are different product systems with protection-only relationships. Metal-to-substrate junctions should be caulked before painting. No edge work within this spec — all adjacent surfaces are separate specs.

affected_conditions.notes: Access modifier applies to ALL metal tasks at elevation. Gutter work is typically at ladder height. Second-story railing work may require scaffold. Ground-floor railings and misc items at ground level = 1.00.

values.surface_rust: Mechanical removal (SP 2/3) or rust conversion + prime

affected_conditions.notes: Rust condition is assessed per component during the condition assessment task. Surface rust is treatable. Structural rot is a hard stop requiring client notification.

excluded_conditions.rationale: Environmental conditions are important to the metal painting PROCESS but are NOT estimatable. They are unpredictable, change daily, and cannot be set as fixed conditions for an estimate. Per established exterior spec convention.

excluded.reason: Unpredictable. Changes hourly. Cannot set a fixed modifier for estimate.
Metal surfaces in direct sun can exceed 140 degrees F. Varies by time of day. Not predictable at bid time.
Weather-dependent. Not predictable at bid time.
Flash rust risk on freshly cleaned steel in high humidity. Scheduling concern, not estimation.

valid_input_states.rationale: Five input states cover both NC and existing metal. SS_EXT_BARE_METAL = new uncoated metal (bare steel, new galvanized, bare aluminum). SS_EXT_PRIMED_FACTORY = factory-primed NC metal (most railings ship primed). SS_EXT_SURFACE_RUST = existing steel/iron with treatable surface rust. SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT_METAL = existing metal with adhered paint in good condition. SS_EXT_FAILING_PAINT_METAL = existing metal with peeling, cracking, or alligatored paint.

output_state.rationale: Output state is the painted finish. Semi-gloss is the most common exterior metal sheen (moisture shedding, durability, ease of cleaning). Gloss for QT5 ornamental. Satin acceptable at QT3.

adjacent_state_protection_analysis.rationale: DTM metal paint drips/overspray on finished siding is difficult to remove (different product chemistry). Full cover for finished siding. Light mask for unfinished — metal paint splatter on bare wood will be covered by siding primer/paint.
Masonry texture hides minor splatter. Light mask at junction if masonry is finished. No protection needed on unfinished masonry — it will be painted later.
Fascia directly behind gutters — highest drip risk during gutter painting. Full mask if finished. Unfinished fascia needs no protection.

exterior_substrate_states.description: New, uncoated metal surface. Includes bare carbon steel, bare wrought iron, new galvanized steel, and bare aluminum. Each substrate type has different prep and primer requirements despite sharing this state designation.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: SP 1 solvent clean (ALL substrates). Carbon steel/iron: SP 2-3 to remove mill scale and light oxidation, prime with DTM acrylic or alkyd. Aluminum: light abrade with scotch-brite or 120-grit, prime within 15 minutes with etch primer or acrylic bonding primer. Galvanized: remove passivation oils (newly galvanized) or white rust (partially weathered), etch primer.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Substrate-dependent. Steel/iron: DTM acrylic (standard) or DTM alkyd, zinc-rich (QT5), epoxy (marginal prep). Aluminum: etch/wash primer or acrylic bonding. Galvanized: etch/wash primer or acrylic bonding. BLOCK oil/alkyd on galvanized and aluminum.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: NC state. Substrate_type dimension determines which primer system is used. This single state covers multiple substrate types with different primer pathways.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Factory-primed metal (most NC railings, some gutters). Factory primer provides transit protection only — field coating still required. Factory primer is typically a thin shop coat, not a full corrosion-inhibitive system.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: SP 1 solvent clean. Verify factory primer adhesion (cross-hatch tape test). Light abrade with 120-grit or scotch-brite for adhesion profile. Touch up any damaged/bare spots with field primer.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Field primer NOT required if factory primer adhesion is verified. Touch-up primer for damaged spots only. Full field prime if factory primer fails adhesion test.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: NC state. Factory-primed metal is the most common NC scenario for railings. Two finish coats over verified factory primer.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Existing steel or iron with treatable surface rust. Thin, flaky oxide layer. Metal substrate structurally sound underneath. NOT applicable to aluminum or galvanized (they do not rust in the traditional sense — aluminum oxidizes, galvanized develops white rust).
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: SP 1 solvent clean. Assess rust depth — surface rust (treatable) vs structural rot (HARD STOP). Mechanical removal (SP 2/SP 3) or rust conversion depending on complexity. Prime exposed bare metal with DTM primer. Feather edges of any sound adjacent paint.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: DTM acrylic primer on mechanically prepped bare metal. Rust converter + DTM primer on conversion-treated areas. Epoxy primer for marginal surfaces.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Existing/repaint state for steel and iron only. Structural rust is a HARD STOP — not a state, but a gate condition.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Existing metal with adhered paint in good condition. No rust, no peeling, no cracking. Maintenance recoat scenario.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: SP 1 solvent clean. Light abrade for adhesion profile (120-grit or scotch-brite). Spot-prime any bare or thinned areas. Clean dust.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Spot prime only where needed. Full prime not required on sound existing paint.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Existing/repaint state. Easiest prep scenario — clean, abrade, topcoat.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Existing metal with failing paint — peeling, cracking, alligatored, or chalking coating. May have rust at failure points on steel/iron substrates.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: SP 1 solvent clean. Mechanical removal (SP 2/SP 3) of all loose and failing paint. Feather edges to sound paint. Treat any exposed rust (mechanical or conversion). Prime all bare metal areas. May require full strip on severely failed surfaces.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: DTM acrylic primer on all exposed bare metal. Full prime recommended if > 30% of surface required stripping.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Existing/repaint state. Most labor-intensive scenario — essentially restarting the coating system on failed areas.

exterior_access_type_analysis.treatment: Modifier on tasks, not a site condition. Same concept as FAC_HEIGHT for interior.

scenarios.notes: Ground-floor railings, low fences, mailbox posts. Baseline rate.
Gutter work at eave height, second-story railing components. Constant repositioning for linear runs.
Extended gutter runs at height, multi-story ornamental iron. Better ergonomics than ladder for detailed metalwork. Setup/teardown is a separate line item.
Third-story gutters, cupola ironwork, difficult access points. Requires firm ground for equipment. Rental cost separate.

exterior_environmental_constraints.note: Environmental constraints are documented here for SOP reference but are EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers per established exterior spec convention.

sop_reference_only.go_threshold: < 10 mph for spray operations on metal
sop_reference_only.optimal: Calm to light breeze for brush work

sop_reference_only.note: Metal in direct sun can exceed 140F. Below 50: slow cure, poor adhesion. Above 90: rapid flash-off, poor film formation, blistering.

sop_reference_only.rule: Surface temp must be >= 5 degrees F above dew point
sop_reference_only.note: Metal surfaces cool faster than ambient — high dew point risk in early morning.
High humidity causes flash rust on freshly cleaned steel within hours. Clean and prime same day.

sop_reference_only.rule: Cleaned bare steel/iron must be primed within 4-8 hours (less in high humidity)
sop_reference_only.note: Flash rust forms on bare steel in hours. If flash rust appears, re-clean before priming.

railing_simple_brush.notes: Simple picket railing, brush application. Includes both sides of pickets, top rail, bottom rail per LF. Standard complexity 1.0x.

railing_spray_backbrush.notes: Spray + back-brush on simple railing. 2-person crew. Faster for long straight runs. Back-brush for crevice coverage.

railing_ornate_brush.notes: Ornate scrollwork, historic ironwork. Brush only. 2.0-3.0x complexity multiplier already embedded in rate.

gutter_brush.notes: Exterior face of gutters. Straight runs. Simple profile. At ladder height typically.

gutter_spray.notes: Spray application on gutter exterior face. Faster for long runs. Overspray protection required for roof and siding.

downspout_brush.notes: Downspout painting, brush. Round or rectangular profile. At various heights.

ornamental_discrete_ea.notes: Discrete ornamental items (finials, rosettes, scroll elements). Per-piece basis. Highly variable by complexity.

misc_item_ea.notes: Miscellaneous items — mailbox posts, light poles, utility covers. Highly variable by size and complexity.

sp1_solvent_clean.notes: Solvent wipe down. Rate for railing-type profiles. Flat gutter runs faster.

sp2_hand_tool.notes: Wire brush, scraper. Remove loose rust and paint. Rate for railing profiles.

sp3_power_tool.notes: Angle grinder with wire wheel or flap disc. Remove moderate rust. Slower on complex profiles.

rust_conversion.notes: Apply converter, wait 15-30 min, verify. Efficient for intricate surfaces. Includes wait time.

primer_brush.notes: Brush primer on railing-type profiles. Same rate as finish coat.

primer_spray.notes: Spray primer on railing runs. Back-brush for crevice coverage.

caulk_metal_junctions.notes: Caulk metal-to-masonry or metal-to-wood junctions. Polyurethane sealant. Gun + tool.

key_decisions.topic: Combined NC and existing metal in one spec
key_decisions.decision: This spec covers BOTH new construction and existing metal surfaces. Not NC-only.
key_decisions.rationale: Metal painting commonly involves existing surfaces (rusted railings, aging gutters). The core painting workflow is similar regardless of substrate state — only prep intensity differs. Substrate state dimension handles branching. Spec name is SF_METAL_EXT_v1 (no NC).

key_decisions.decision: Four paintable items: ITM_METAL_RAILING (LF), ITM_METAL_GUTTER (LF), ITM_METAL_ORNAMENTAL (EA or LF), ITM_METAL_MISC (EA).
key_decisions.rationale: Each component has dramatically different production rates, access conditions, complexity profiles, and counting methods. Gutters at 100-150 LF/hr vs scrollwork at 5-10 LF/hr — cannot use a single rate. Component-based estimation is mandatory.

key_decisions.topic: Substrate type as primary configuration dimension
key_decisions.decision: Include substrate_type dimension: carbon_steel, wrought_iron, aluminum, galvanized.
key_decisions.rationale: Substrate type drives primer selection, prep constraints, coating flexibility requirements, and material blocker rules. Wrong primer on wrong substrate = catastrophic failure (saponification on galvanized, oxide adhesion failure on aluminum).

key_decisions.decision: Quality tier dimension: QT3, QT4, QT5. QT2 excluded.
key_decisions.rationale: Metal prep shortcuts lead to rapid coating failure. QT2's economy approach (reduced prep) is inappropriate for metal substrates where prep is 60-80% of coating longevity. QT3 is the minimum acceptable tier. QT5 applies to ornamental/architectural ironwork.

key_decisions.topic: Profile complexity as modifier, not dimension
key_decisions.decision: Profile complexity (standard/moderate/ornate) is a MODIFIER applied per component, not a configuration dimension.
key_decisions.rationale: A single project may have standard railings, moderate gutters, and ornate gate — complexity varies by component, not project-wide. Multiplier: standard 1.0x, moderate 1.5x, ornate 2.0-3.0x.

key_decisions.topic: SSPC prep level determined by condition, not chosen independently
key_decisions.decision: SSPC prep standard is determined by substrate condition assessment, not offered as an independent selection dimension.
key_decisions.rationale: Prep level is a technical decision based on rust severity, substrate condition, and quality tier — not a customer choice. Light surface rust = SP 2-3. Heavy rust = SP 3-SP 7. Critical QT5 = SP 10-11. Including it as a choosable dimension would create invalid combinations.

key_decisions.decision: Oil/alkyd products BLOCKED for galvanized substrate. Rigid/brittle coatings BLOCKED for aluminum substrate.
key_decisions.rationale: Galvanized + oil/alkyd = saponification (catastrophic). Aluminum + rigid coating = thermal cracking at expansion joints. These must be enforced as material blocker rules, not advisory notes.

key_decisions.topic: Structural rust as hard stop, not substrate state
key_decisions.decision: Structural rust/rot is a HARD STOP assessment gate, not a treatable substrate state.
key_decisions.rationale: Structural rot (deep pitting, crumbling metal, loss of cross-section) is outside painting scope. It requires welding, reinforcement, or replacement. Including it as a substrate state would imply it can be treated within this spec.

key_decisions.topic: Brush as primary application method for metal
key_decisions.decision: Brush is the primary/default application method for most metal components. Spray is supplemental for flat runs.
key_decisions.rationale: Unlike wall/siding specs where spray is primary, metal's complex profiles (pickets, balusters, rivets, crevices) demand brush detail work for proper coverage. Spray_backbrush for railing runs. Spray for straight gutter runs. No roll option — rollers are ineffective on cylindrical profiles.

key_decisions.decision: EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers. Per established exterior spec convention.
key_decisions.rationale: Environmental conditions (wind, surface temp, humidity, flash rust risk) are unpredictable at bid time. Documented for SOP/field reference only.

key_decisions.topic: Rust treatment method as condition-driven, not dimension
key_decisions.decision: Rust treatment method (mechanical vs conversion) is determined by surface complexity and condition, not offered as an independent dimension.
key_decisions.rationale: Ornate scrollwork may REQUIRE conversion (mechanical prep impossible in crevices). Flat railings should use mechanical removal for longer life. The choice is a technical/SOP decision, not a customer selection.

key_decisions.decision: QT3/QT4: 1 primer + 2 finish coats. QT5: zinc-rich or epoxy primer + DTM acrylic topcoat (may include intermediate coat for 3-coat system on critical steel). Factory-primed NC: 2 finish coats (skip primer if adhesion test passes).
key_decisions.rationale: Metal coating system must provide both corrosion protection (primer) and UV/weather protection (topcoat). Two finish coats provide proper DFT build. QT5 premium primer systems (zinc-rich, epoxy) add corrosion protection layer.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: PRIMARY DIMENSION. Drives primer selection, prep constraints, material blocker rules, and coating flexibility requirements. Not captured by existing PS keys.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Per-component if mixed substrates on same project (e.g., steel railing + aluminum gutters). May need per-item substrate assignment.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Drives substrate state assignment and prep module selection. Per-component assessment.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Maps to the five substrate states. 'structural_rot' is a HARD STOP assessment, not a selectable condition value.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Per-component labor multiplier. Standard 1.0x, moderate 1.5x, ornate 2.0-3.0x. Not captured by existing PS keys.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Applied per component — a project may have mixed complexity across different metal items.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: LF of roof edge requiring protection during gutter painting. Drop cloth or plastic along roof shingle line at gutter. Unique to gutter scope — no equivalent in wall/siding specs.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Only relevant when gutter painting is in scope.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: SF of masonry wall requiring protection behind railings or near downspout runs during metal painting. May exist in other specs — check before creating.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Spray operations on metal near masonry walls require masonry protection.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Environmental conditions (wind, temp, humidity) might be estimatable modifiers for metal work
research_corrections.corrected_to: Environmental conditions EXCLUDED from estimation per established exterior spec convention.
research_corrections.rationale: Same convention as masonry, siding, and deck siblings. Environmental conditions are unpredictable at bid time.

research_corrections.corrected_to: Landscape protection is LF-based — measured along perimeter where landscape is adjacent to metal work area.
research_corrections.rationale: Per established exterior spec convention. LF along perimeter, not SF of landscape area.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Standard NC research correction excludes condition modifier
research_corrections.corrected_to: Condition assessment IS relevant for this spec because it covers both NC and existing metal. Substrate condition (bare, factory-primed, surface rust, sound paint, failing paint) drives prep module selection.
research_corrections.rationale: Unlike pure NC specs where substrate state is known (bare or factory-primed), this spec handles existing metal with variable conditions. Condition assessment is a required estimation input.

research_corrections.topic: SSPC prep level as dimension vs condition-driven
research_corrections.original_assumption: SSPC prep level (SP1-SP11) offered as an independent configuration dimension per user brief
research_corrections.corrected_to: SSPC prep level is determined by substrate condition and quality tier, not offered as an independent dimension.
research_corrections.rationale: Prep level is a technical decision, not a customer choice. Including it as a choosable dimension creates invalid combinations (e.g., SP 11 blast on an aluminum gutter makes no sense). The spec determines appropriate prep from condition + QT.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Standard exterior application methods (brush, roll, spray) apply to metal
research_corrections.corrected_to: Roll method EXCLUDED for metal. Brush is primary, spray supplemental. No roll option.
research_corrections.rationale: Rollers are ineffective on cylindrical and complex metal profiles (pickets, balusters, downspouts, scrollwork). Brush provides crevice coverage. Spray provides speed for flat runs. Roll has no practical application on metal components.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Standard QT2-QT5 quality tier range applies
research_corrections.corrected_to: QT2 excluded. QT3 is the minimum tier for metal work.
research_corrections.rationale: Metal prep shortcuts (reduced cleaning, skipped SP steps, economy primer) lead to rapid coating failure. Metal coating longevity is 60-80% prep-dependent. Economy prep is not a viable option for metal substrates.

assumptions.value: Exterior metal painting — railings, gutters, downspouts, ornamental iron, miscellaneous metal items. Covers BOTH new construction and existing/maintenance metal. Residential scope.
assumptions.note: Spec name SF_METAL_EXT_v1 (no NC) reflects dual-scope coverage. Structural steel, industrial metal, and commercial metal are out of scope.

assumptions.value: Stainless steel excluded from primary scope — rarely painted in residential context.
assumptions.note: Stainless steel hardware (handrails, fixtures) is typically left uncoated. If painting is needed, etch primer protocol from aluminum pathway applies.

assumptions.value: Factory powder-coated metal recoating excluded from primary scope.
assumptions.note: Powder coat adhesion testing and prep protocol not covered in metal surfaces doctrine. Could be added as a future substrate state if demand warrants.

assumptions.value: QT2 not applicable to metal work — minimum tier is QT3.
assumptions.note: Metal coating longevity is 60-80% prep-dependent. Economy prep (QT2 pattern) leads to rapid failure. The cost of premature recoat exceeds savings from reduced prep.

assumptions.value: Roll application method excluded — not practical for metal component profiles.
assumptions.note: Cylindrical pickets, round downspouts, complex scrollwork profiles make rollers impractical. Brush and spray are the only viable methods.

uncertainties.detail: Doctrine provides 5-10 LF/hr for ornate scrollwork but this is a wide range. Actual rate depends heavily on specific pattern complexity, crevice depth, and whether pieces are in-situ or removable. Historic ironwork with hand-forged scroll patterns may be slower than 5 LF/hr.
uncertainties.recommendation: Use 7 LF/hr as baseline for ornate. Flag for field calibration on first ornamental project. Consider per-EA pricing for highly variable ornamental pieces.

uncertainties.topic: Rust conversion life expectancy in residential context
uncertainties.detail: Doctrine states 1-3 year life for rust conversion vs 4-5x for mechanical removal. This is a significant range. Actual life depends on exposure conditions, coating system quality, and conversion product quality. In sheltered locations (covered porch), conversion may perform closer to 3 years.
uncertainties.recommendation: Document conversion as shorter-life option in project record. Quote mechanical removal as default for QT4/QT5. Conversion acceptable for QT3 or where mechanical prep is physically impossible.

uncertainties.detail: Projects with mixed metal substrates (e.g., steel railing + aluminum gutters + galvanized downspouts) require multiple primer types. This adds material complexity and cost. Doctrine does not provide guidance on minimum order quantities or waste factors for multi-primer projects.
uncertainties.recommendation: Track primer quantities separately per substrate type. Flag multi-substrate projects for material manager review. Minimum 1 QT primer per substrate type even for small areas.

uncertainties.topic: Spray overspray waste on narrow metal profiles
uncertainties.detail: Spraying narrow targets (pickets, downspouts, railings) generates significant overspray compared to spraying wall field. Doctrine's 25-33% spray waste factor is for wall/siding applications. Metal spray waste may be 30-50% due to small target profiles.
uncertainties.recommendation: Use 35% spray waste factor for metal profiles as baseline. Flag for field calibration. Brush application avoids waste entirely — factor into method selection for small projects.
